entities.summary:
The human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) is a retrovirus that attacks the immune system. Without treatment, it can lead to a spectrum of conditions including acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS). It is a preventable disease. It can be managed with treatment and become a manageable chronic health condition. While there is no cure or vaccine for HIV, antiretroviral treatment can slow the course of the disease, and, if used before significant disease progression, can extend the life expectancy of those infected.

HIV/AIDS first emerged in the early 20th century in central Africa. The virus was initially detected in the 1980s and was identified as the cause of AIDS in 1984. Since then, it has become a global pandemic, with millions of people infected worldwide. Despite significant advances in treatment and prevention, HIV/AIDS remains a major public health concern.

The impact of HIV/AIDS has been profound, with millions of people dying from the disease and many more affected by it. However, the global response to the epidemic has also been significant, with the development of antiretroviral therapy and other treatments that have improved the lives of those living with HIV. The legacy of HIV/AIDS will continue to be felt for generations to come, shaping the way we understand and respond to infectious diseases.

It is estimated that over 70 million people have been infected with HIV since the beginning of the epidemic, with over 35 million people dying from the disease. As of 2020, there were over 38 million people living with HIV, with the majority of those in sub-Saharan Africa.
